issue: The caption's 'successive, not jointly retained' disclaimer is attached to the recurrent row but the figure's own note applies 'snapshots are schematic' to both rows, inviting the reader to misapply it to the KV row; the figure also does not name the model the caption cites.

issue: The caption's proportionality sentence is incoherent, and its exclusion list omits the NVFP4 per-tensor FP32 global scale that the figure itself flags as outside the 18 B local total.

The figure states 'NVFP4 global FP32 scale: 4 B per tensor, not per block', but the caption's exclusion list ('padding, headers, extra copies and high-precision exceptions') does not include it, so a reader may add the 4 B to the 18 B total or may not, with no guidance. Including it would give 22 B / 32 = 0.6875 B/value = 5.5 bit/value.

issue: The subtitle says '140 GB tensor' while the x-axis says 'Logical input tensor per rank [GB]'; the per-rank qualifier is dropped exactly where the reader needs it to interpret the 1.75× factor.

acceptance_test: Change the subtitle to '140 GB per rank (245 GB sent at 1.75×)' so that the subtitle, the x-axis, and the caption use one qualifier.

issue: The figure asserts the 1.75× traffic factor without showing where it comes from, so the reader must take it on faith or reconstruct it from the caption.
evidence: Subtitle: 'sent bytes per rank = 1.75 × tensor bytes'. The factor is 2(N−1)/N = 2×7/8 = 1.75 for N=8 (reduce-scatter plus all-gather, each moving (N−1)/N of the tensor). Neither the figure nor the caption states this; the caption only says 'Each rank sends 1.75 times the logical tensor size and receives the same amount.' The same unexplained constant appears in FIG 9.2 as '12 B sent' for an 8 B input (1.5× at N=4).
acceptance_test: Add the derivation to the subtitle, e.g. 'sent bytes per rank = 2(N−1)/N × tensor = 1.75 × tensor bytes', and mirror the same form in FIG 9.2's summary box ('12 B sent = 1.5 × 8 B input').

figure: FIG 9.2 phase annotations ('3 neighbor rounds / 6 B sent + 6 B received/rank')
issue: '3 neighbor rounds' can be misread as '3 neighbors', but a four-rank ring has exactly two distinct neighbors per rank; the quantity being counted is rounds (steps), not neighbors.
evidence: The figure's own ring sub-diagram shows R0→R1→R2→R3→R0, i.e. two neighbors per rank. The correct count is 3 rounds (N−1 steps) per phase, each moving one 2 B chunk, as the separate note 'Each rank sends one 2 B chunk to the next rank' states.
acceptance_test: Change both phase annotations to '3 rounds (one 2 B chunk per round)' or '3 steps × 2 B = 6 B sent per rank', so that rounds and neighbors are not conflated.

figure: FIG 9.2 reduce-scatter row (Rank 0 → [10], Rank 1 → [20], Rank 2 → [-10], Rank 3 → [0])
issue: The figure asserts a specific chunk→rank ownership (rank r ends with reduced chunk r) without stating the chunk-flow convention, and the most commonly taught forward-flow convention yields rank r → chunk r+1. An expert reader who knows that convention will read the figure as wrong rather than as a convention choice.
evidence: With the textbook convention 'at step 0 rank r forwards its own chunk r to its successor', chunk j starts at rank j and completes at rank j−1, so rank r would hold chunk r+1 (rank 0 → 20, rank 1 → −10, rank 2 → 0, rank 3 → 10). The figure's assignment is nevertheless achievable — it corresponds to the variant where rank r forwards chunk r−1 first, so chunk j starts at rank j+1 and completes at rank j — but the figure shows only the neighbour order, not the chunk flow, so the reader cannot tell which convention is in force.
acceptance_test: Add one clause to the caption or the figure, e.g. 'chunk j is first forwarded by rank j+1, so rank r ends the reduce-scatter holding reduced chunk r', or annotate the ring sub-diagram with the chunk index in flight. Confirm that the stated convention reproduces the four reduce-scatter outputs shown.

acceptance_test: Increase the vertical gap between the dashed control path and the launcher box's top border to at least one text-line height, or route the dashed path so that it visibly enters the launcher box from both sides. Re-render at 150 dpi and confirm the two rules are separable at print size.

issue: A single horizontal arrow labeled 'time (decode steps / iterations) ->' spans the full width of the figure, running under both the discrete and the continuous panels. The two panels are separate illustrations on unrelated scales (the discrete panel's rows all start at the same x; the continuous panel's rows are staggered diagonally), so one shared axis implies a common timeline and a common scale that does not exist. As printed, the first factor is a rate, so the product has units GB*req/s^2 and cannot equal a bandwidth. The page-190 note states the correct form ('35 GB/request x 40 req/s = 1.4 TB/s'), so the figure and the note disagree in form. (Reading taken from the 150 dpi render; confirm against the source.)
evidence: Rendered caveat line on PDF 212 / printed 192 versus the Note 11.3-1 text on PDF 210 / printed 190: '35 GB/request x 40 req/s = 1.4 TB/s against the shared fabric'. The figure's first factor appears as '35 GB/s'.

Verify against the source .tex and re-render; if the source already reads '35 GB x 40 req/s', no change is required and this finding is void.

figure: FIGURE 11.3 (caption, token count vs KV size)
issue: The caption pairs a token count with a KV size that do not reconcile at the book's canonical KV rate. As rendered, the caption says 'the canonical 9.8K-token request carries ~24.1 GB'. At the canonical 2.62 MB/token (FP16, full-MHA 70B reference), 24.1 GB corresponds to 24,100/2.62 = 9,198 tokens, i.e. the canonical 9,200-token request (1,200 + 8,000), not 9.8K; a 9.8K-token request would carry 9,800 x 2.62 MB = 25.7 GB. One of the two numbers is wrong wherever this pair appears.
evidence: Rendered caption: 'the canonical 9.8K-token request carries ~24.1 GB'. A reader who glances at the figure (or who sees only the figure, as in a slide or a skim) learns "many arrows vs few arrows," not "materialize-then-re-read vs never materialize."

figure: FIGURE 15.2(a) — Prefill work vs average prefix reuse
issue: The y-axis label "Prefill FLOPs / req (M)" contradicts the caption, which describes the same quantity as "as a percent of no-cache prefill." Read literally, the axis asserts that a no-cache request costs 100 MFLOPs of prefill. That is off by roughly six orders of magnitude from any real LLM (the canonical 1,200-token prefill on a 70B model is ~1.7×10^14 FLOPs, i.e. ~168 TFLOPs, not 100 MFLOPs). A reader who quotes the axis as an absolute figure will be wrong by a factor of ~10^6; a reader who reads the caption will be right. The figure and its caption currently describe two different quantities.
evidence: Rendered page, PDF 259: y-axis reads "Prefill FLOPs / req (M)" with ticks 0–100 and the "no cache" series flat at exactly 100. Caption: "(left: prefill work vs average prefix reuse, as a percent of no-cache prefill, lower is better ...)". The two readings are mutually exclusive: 100 MFLOPs/req is not 100% of no-cache prefill for any model in the book.
acceptance_test: Choose one quantity and make axis and caption agree. Preferred: relabel the axis "Prefill work per request (% of no-cache)" (or "Prefill FLOPs / req (relative; no-cache = 100)") and delete the "(M)". Re-render and confirm no absolute FLOP unit appears on this axis, and that the caption's "percent of no-cache prefill" matches the axis text verbatim.

issue: The figure title asserts the self-host line "crosses the managed API at the canonical 6.24M req/mo," but the figure's own annotation says "break-even ≈ 7.5M," and the arithmetic says no crossing occurs at 6.24M: at 6.24M req/mo the managed API at $20.80/1K costs $129,792/mo, which is BELOW the self-host line of $155,816.93/mo. The self-host line crosses the managed mid-price line at 155,816.93 × 1000 / 20.80 = 7.49M req/mo. The only reading under which the title is defensible is "enters the managed price band" (band entry at $25/1K is 6.23M), but the verb "crosses" and the phrase "at the canonical 6.24M req/mo" both assert a crossing point that the figure contradicts. This is the takeaway sentence of the chapter's central figure.
evidence: Rendered page, PDF 294: caption title line reads "... crosses the managed API at the canonical 6.24M req/mo." In-figure annotation reads "break-even ≈ 7.5M" with a vertical dotted line at that x. Caption body: "the managed API at the canonical 6.24M volume ($129,792/mo vs $87.6K/mo)" — i.e. managed is cheaper than self-host at the canonical volume. Recomputation: 6,240,000/1000 × $20.80 = $129,792 < $155,816.93; break-even V = 155,816.93 × 1000 / 20.80 = 7,491,199 ≈ 7.5M. Band entry at $25/1K: 155,816.93 × 1000 / 25 = 6,232,677 ≈ 6.23M.
acceptance_test: Rewrite the title to state the crossing unambiguously, e.g. "... enters the managed-API price band at ~6.2M req/mo and exits it at ~10.4M (mid-band break-even ≈ 7.5M), i.e. the canonical 6.24M volume sits at the bottom edge of the band." Re-render and confirm the title contains no claim of a crossing at 6.24M, and that the title's numbers agree with the in-figure "break-even ≈ 7.5M" and the caption's $129,792/mo figure.

figure: FIGURE 15.2(a) — Prefill work vs average prefix reuse (in-figure annotation)
issue: The figure's own parameters are undefined and insufficient to reproduce the curve. The annotation reads "f(r)=5/(1+r); P=40%, S=60%" but the caption never defines P or S, and the plotted curve is not f(r) — it is 100·[S + P·f(r)/f(1)], i.e. 60 + 80/(1+r). The normalization by f(1)=2.5 and the combination rule are both unstated, so a reader who tries to reproduce the curve from the annotation gets 5/(1+r) and cannot match the drawing. The reader also cannot tell why the curve floors at ~60 rather than 0 (the S=60% non-cacheable share of prefill), which is the single most decision-relevant feature of the curve.
evidence: Rendered page, PDF 259: annotation "f(r)=5/(1+r); P=40%, S=60%". Caption describes only the axes and the meaning of "average prefix reuse"; it never mentions P, S, or f. Recomputation against the drawn curve: 100·[0.6 + 0.4·(5/(1+r))/(5/2)] = 60 + 80/(1+r) gives r=1→100, r=2→86.7, r=3→80, r=5→73.3, r=10→67.3, r=100→60.8, matching the drawn green curve (which flattens at ~60). The unnormalized f(r)=5/(1+r) would give 2.5 at r=1 and 0.05 at r=100, which does not match.
acceptance_test: Either (a) put the full formula in the figure annotation, e.g. "prefill work = S + P·f(r)/f(1); f(r)=5/(1+r), f(1)=2.5; P=40% cacheable, S=60% not cacheable", or (b) move the formula into the caption and define P and S there in words. Acceptance: a reader with only the figure and its caption can state what P and S mean, can reproduce the curve at r=1, 10 and 100, and can explain the ~60% floor.

issue: The red annotation "break-even ≈ 7.5M" floats at the far left of the plot (roughly x=10^5) with no leader line or other anchor to the vertical dotted line at 7.5M that it labels, and it reads as THE break-even. This is in tension with the caption's explicit statement "the break-even stays a region, not a point" and with the adjacent annotation "sensitivity = 6.2–10.4M (a region, not a point)." The figure therefore simultaneously asserts a point break-even and a region break-even, and the reader must guess which geometry the 7.5M label refers to.
evidence: Rendered page, PDF 294: red text "break-even ≈ 7.5M" sits at the left of the axes, ~2 decades in x from the vertical dotted line at 7.5M; no connector is drawn (contrast the blue "canonical 6.24M req/mo" label, which does have an arrow to the green diamond). Caption: "The break-even region (6.2–10.4M) and the canonical 6.24M point sit inside the feasible band ... The break-even stays a region, not a point."
acceptance_test: Relabel to "mid-band break-even ≈ 7.5M" and add a leader line (or place the label immediately left of the 7.5M dotted line at the line's own y-position). Acceptance: the label is visually attached to the 7.5M line, and no text in the figure asserts a single-valued break-even without the word "mid-band".

issue: Two visual-encoding problems in one figure. (a) The managed mid-price line ($20.80/1K) is drawn in the same red as the price band and runs parallel to the band's diagonal hatch strokes, so at print size the dashed mid-price line is difficult to separate from the band it sits inside — the reader cannot easily locate the $20.80/1K line that the legend names. (b) Grayscale distinguishability: the price band (red diagonal hatch) and the INFEASIBLE region (a second diagonal hatch fill) are encoded by the same visual device, differing mainly in fill density and hue. In grayscale the two hatched regions are confusable, and the reader may read the right-hand infeasible wedge as part of the price band.
evidence: Rendered page, PDF 294: legend swatches show "price band $15–25/1K" as a red diagonal hatch and "managed $20.80/1K" as a red dashed line; in the plot the dashed line runs up-right inside a band whose hatch strokes also run up-right. The region right of the 24.96M dotted line carries a second diagonal hatch fill of similar orientation. Both the band and the infeasible wedge are the only hatched areas in the figure.
acceptance_test: Give the mid-price line a distinct encoding (different color, or a heavier dash pattern, or a different hatch angle for the band) and give the INFEASIBLE region a fill that is not a diagonal hatch (e.g. a flat light gray with a solid boundary). Acceptance: (i) in a grayscale conversion at 150 dpi the $20.80/1K line is traceable from the legend to the plot without ambiguity; (ii) the infeasible wedge is identifiable as a distinct region without relying on the red "INFEASIBLE" text label.

issue: The x-axis mixes two rate bases without saying so. The caption states that the workload points are placed at "x = 10 rps average × duration," while the feasible-max boundary is "capacity 40 rps × 624,000 = 24.96M req/mo." The canonical point (6.24M) and the feasible max (24.96M) are therefore the SAME workload duration (624,000 s) at two different rates, not two volumes of the same workload. The axis label ("Requests/month (log) — duration varied at FIXED 40 rps peak, FIXED 21-host fleet") does not disclose this, so a reader can conclude that 24.96M req/mo is feasible for the canonical workload shape — which would require 2,496,000 active seconds, four times the 624,000 s window. The caption carries the correction; the figure does not.
evidence: Rendered page, PDF 294: x-axis label "Requests/month (log) — duration varied at FIXED 40 rps peak, FIXED 21-host fleet". Caption assumptions: "x = 10 rps average × duration (for the workload points) ... feasible max = capacity 40 rps × 624,000 = 24.96M req/mo." Recomputation: 6,240,000 / 10 rps = 624,000 s (canonical duration); 24,960,000 / 10 rps = 2,496,000 s, which exceeds the 624,000 s active window by 4×.
acceptance_test: State the rate basis on the axis or in an in-figure note, e.g. "Requests/month (log) — workload points at 10 rps avg × duration; feasible max = 40 rps sustained × 624,000 s". Acceptance: the figure alone makes it impossible to read 24.96M as the same-workload volume that the canonical 6.24M point represents.
